benjamin-strong-and-the-coup-de-whiskey-.context_blurb:
Benjamin Strong, a New York banker who had attended the secret 1910 meeting on Jekyll Island that sketched out the Federal Reserve, became the first governor of the New York Fed in 1914. Until his death in October 1928 he was the strongest personality in the young central bank. Austrian economists later saw his easy money as a root of the 1929 crash.

The Fed's chief power is over how much money circulates. When it creates a great deal of new money and pushes it into the economy, prices in the shops tend to rise, because more money is chasing the same goods. Strong pioneered the Fed's most important everyday tool, open market operations: buying Treasury bonds from banks to add reserves and push rates down, and selling them to drain reserves away.

His closest friend in finance was Montagu Norman, who governed the Bank of England for twenty-four years, from 1920 to 1944, one of the longest reigns of any central banker, and together they shaped world monetary policy through the decade. In 1925 Britain, with Winston Churchill as Chancellor of the Exchequer, went back onto gold at the prewar parity of about $4.86 to the pound. That rate overvalued the pound and brought painful deflation, strikes and unemployment, and John Maynard Keynes attacked the decision in a famous pamphlet. To help his friend, Strong kept American rates low so gold would not drain from London to New York.

In July 1927 Strong gathered Europe's central bankers in secret at an estate on Long Island. Montagu Norman of the Bank of England and Hjalmar Schacht of Germany's Reichsbank came in person, and the Bank of France, governed by Émile Moreau, sent its deputy governor, Charles Rist. Days later the Fed trimmed its discount rate, the price of its loans to banks, by half a point to 3.5 percent, to help the Europeans keep their currencies tied to gold. In private, Strong reportedly said the cut would give the stock market a little coup de whiskey. The phrase survives through the later Senate testimony of Adolph Miller, the one Fed Board member who opposed the cut.

Austrian economics explains why such a cut is dangerous. An interest rate held below the level where saving and borrowing would naturally meet tells a business owner, falsely, that people want to save more, so long-term projects such as new factories look profitable. Murray Rothbard's America's Great Depression (1963) traced the crash to the Fed's credit expansion from 1921 to 1929, when the money supply grew by roughly 60 percent, and once Strong died nobody at the Fed could rein it in. Austrians call the wasteful projects that cheap credit funded, ventures doomed once the boom ended, malinvestment.

Those who fault the 1927 cut argue that the cheap money that poured into New York fueled a stock-market bubble that burst in October 1929 and opened the Great Depression. The episode teaches one move about central banks acting in concert. When they ease together to defend a fixed exchange rate, the country doing the easing can get inflated asset prices even if its own economy needs no easing at all: Strong eased Britain's problem and created America's.

bootleggers-and-baptists-bruce-yandle-19.context_blurb:
Bruce Yandle, an economist from Clemson University, served as executive director of the Federal Trade Commission in the early 1980s and kept noticing an odd alliance behind new regulations. In 1983 he described it in a short essay for Regulation magazine, subtitled The Education of a Regulatory Economist. His two-word name for the alliance became one of the most-cited ideas in political economy.

Two groups with clashing motives can end up quietly wanting the very same rule for opposite reasons. Yandle's model case came from old Sunday liquor bans. Church members backed them because they believed drinking on the Sabbath was wrong, and illegal moonshine sellers backed them because, with the legal stores shut, thirsty customers came to them instead. Yandle named the pattern after that unlikely pair: Bootleggers and Baptists.

In the American South, devout Baptists campaigned loudly for Sunday closing as a moral crusade, while bootleggers profited quietly, because on Sundays their illegal liquor faced no legal competition. The Baptists were the moral partner and the bootleggers the profit partner. Each side needed the other. The bootleggers gained profits and helped pay for the fight, while the Baptists gave the rule moral cover, so that lawmakers could defend it without blushing.

Once seen, the coalition turns up everywhere. When a city tightens the rules on where Uber and Lyft may pick up riders or what they may charge, taxi-medallion holders, who profit from keeping rivals out, usually stand at city hall beside pedestrian-safety advocates, who supply the moral cover. Environmental rules work the same way. Sincere environmentalists support a rule to protect the planet, while domestic producers cheer it on quietly when it burdens foreign competitors more than themselves, so a green rule doubles as a trade barrier.

Economists read the nationwide alcohol ban of the 18th Amendment, which lasted from 1919 to 1933, as the biggest case of all. On one side stood moralists such as the Anti-Saloon League and the Woman's Christian Temperance Union; on the other, organized-crime beneficiaries who ran the black market and grew rich while it lasted. In 2014 Yandle expanded the idea into a full book with a co-author confusingly named Adam Smith, a present-day scholar rather than the Scot of 1776. The Cato Institute published it as Bootleggers and Baptists: How Economic Forces and Moral Persuasion Interact to Shape Regulatory Politics.

Yandle turned the insight into a habit for reading the news. In a working coalition the moral side does the visible lobbying and holds the microphone, while the profit side quietly supplies the resources and signs the checks. Regulatory economists, he wrote, spend years learning to look past the moral rhetoric to find the bootlegger.

bryan-caplan-education-signaling-and-rat.context_blurb:
Bryan Caplan teaches economics at George Mason University and has built a career on book-length arguments against ideas most readers assume are settled. He writes plainly, for educated general readers, and starts from a specific puzzle in the data rather than from a slogan. His targets have included voters, parents, colleges and the rules that keep houses scarce.

His best-known claim concerns college. The bulk of a graduate's higher pay, Caplan argues, comes not from what was learned in class but from what the diploma tells employers: that its holder can finish hard, dull tasks. Economists call this signaling, and The Case Against Education, his book of 2018, presses it hard. If he is right, students will pay a great deal for the degree itself, even when the classes taught them nothing useful, because the paper is what employers reward.

His evidence includes a jump in the data. Someone who quits one class short of graduating earns far less over a lifetime than a classmate who finished, though their coursework barely differs, so the diploma by itself seems to be worth a small fortune. Economists call that jump at the finish line the sheepskin effect. Caplan estimates that roughly 80 percent of the college wage premium is signaling, a claim that is heterodox even among friendly economists, and from it he draws his main policy recommendation: cut education subsidies. The signaling story changes what taxpayers buy. If a degree mostly shows that a student is bright and diligent, then grants, cheap loans and state universities pump up the signal without producing matching productive skills, and as more people hold the same diploma its premium wears away.

His 2007 book, The Myth of the Rational Voter, argued that voters hold systematically biased views on economics, suspicious of markets, of trade with foreigners and of saving, and keep them because a mistaken ballot costs the person casting it nothing. Caplan named the pattern rational irrationality. A shopper who believes nonsense pays for it at the checkout, but a voter who believes nonsense pays nothing, so clear thinking about politics is personally costly and privately worthless. The idea extends an older public-choice claim. In 1957 Anthony Downs argued that voters barely study the issues since one ballot in millions hardly ever decides anything, and he called that rational ignorance; Caplan's addition is that voters not only skip the homework but also indulge comfortable errors.

In 2011 Caplan used research on twins and adopted children to argue that how grown children turn out owes much less to their parents than most people believe, so raising children can be more relaxed than people fear, and he titled the book Selfish Reasons to Have More Kids.

His case for freer immigration rests on a startling gap. With an ox and hand tools, a farmer in a poor land might raise some $500 of crops a year; move that same man to a wealthy nation of tractors, good roads and reliable power, and similar work could pay around $40,000. Where people work, not just how hard they work, sets what they can produce. His 2024 book Build, Baby, Build turned to housing. When a booming city such as San Francisco smothers construction in permits, zoning and neighborhood vetoes while new jobs keep drawing residents, home prices climb steeply, because supply cannot keep pace with demand. Unusually for a tenured professor, Caplan made both of these books nonfiction graphic novels, Open Borders (2019) drawn by Zach Weinersmith and the housing book drawn by Ady Branzei. The comic form solves a problem scholarly prose cannot, reaching general readers who never open an academic book.

capitalism-and-freedom-1962-and-free-to-.context_blurb:
Milton Friedman, the University of Chicago economist who won the Nobel prize in 1976, wrote two books for ordinary readers that went on to change American policy. The first, in 1962, argued that economic and political freedom are bound together and offered a list of reforms that sounded eccentric at the time. The second, in 1980, written with his wife Rose, carried the case to television.

The 1962 book began as talks Friedman delivered in 1956 at Indiana's Wabash College, and Rose helped turn them into plain English. He called it Capitalism and Freedom, and over the years buyers took home upward of 500,000 copies. Its central claim runs in one direction only: economic freedom is necessary for political freedom, though it is not enough by itself. Once a government controls the jobs, the press and the currency, a dissenter cannot hold out, because he cannot even eat.

The book's proposals included vouchers that parents could spend at any school, a negative income tax in place of the tangle of welfare programs, an army of volunteers, floating exchange rates, and an end to licensing rules that kept newcomers out of trades. Universal single-payer health insurance, the Canadian model, was never among them. Ending the draft was the proposal that produced the sharpest exchange. In the late 1960s, at hearings of a presidential commission on the draft, General William Westmoreland objected that he had no wish to lead mercenaries, and Friedman asked whether he would rather have an army of slaves. Congress let the draft authority lapse in 1973.

Free to Choose made the same case through everyday scenes. A shopper choosing freely among thousands of items buys what her family really wants; hand the same budget to a committee of nutrition experts, and many shoppers would end up with food they did not want while the shelves filled with things nobody bought. The 1980 book accompanied a ten-part public-television series shot on location from Hong Kong to Chicago and Washington, and it became the best-selling nonfiction book in America that year. According to Friedman's memoirs, it was smuggled into the Soviet Union and Eastern Europe in underground translations, and the Czech reformer Václav Klaus later credited it as a source of his country's reforms after 1989.

The voucher idea was older than either book. Friedman first set it out in 1955 in an essay, The Role of Government in Education, in a volume edited by Robert Solo, and later folded it into Capitalism and Freedom. He had argued since 1953 for letting currencies float freely against one another. When Richard Nixon closed the gold window in August 1971, the fixed-rate system of Bretton Woods fell apart, and by 1973 the world's major currencies were floating against each other.

Looking back, historians note how many of the 1962 proposals that seemed eccentric at the time became mainstream policy: the volunteer army in 1973, floating currencies in the early 1970s, and state voucher programs from the 1990s on.

ceausescus-romania-and-the-1989-executio.context_blurb:
Nicolae Ceaușescu ruled Romania for twenty-four years from 1965, first as head of its Communist Party and later as head of state as well, with his wife Elena at his side as co-ruler. His regime joined a cult of personality to ruinous central planning. It held together for decades, then collapsed in about a week in December 1989, and he became the only communist leader shot in that year's revolutions.

By the late 1980s Romanians lived with empty shops, secret police everywhere, and heat and electricity doled out for only a few hours daily; what they threw off that December was a communist dictatorship. Ceaușescu's monument was a colossal palace in central Bucharest for the party's ruling bodies, built in the 1980s as the House of the People by 20,000 workers and 700 architects over eight years. Only one office building on earth has more floor space, and a great stretch of the old city, churches included, was flattened to make room. Today it is called the Palace of the Parliament and houses Romania's legislature.

In October 1966 Ceaușescu banned abortion and contraception, both legal since 1957, to drive the birthrate up by command. The order, Decree 770, also taxed unmarried adults and childless couples over twenty-five, and births nearly doubled within a year. The state could not care for the babies it had ordered into the world. When foreign reporters entered Romania's state institutions in 1990, they found about 100,000 children in appalling orphanages, and the footage drove reform of international adoption for decades.

In the 1980s his program of systematization bulldozed thousands of farming villages and herded families out of their old houses into identical concrete blocks near state factories. It was central planning in miniature: one small group decides how everyone should live and ignores what people actually want. The hardship had another cause too. Through the decade Ceaușescu insisted on paying off every dollar of foreign debt, exporting grain, meat and fuel for hard currency, while at home Romanians endured rolling power blackouts and rationed food, queues for meat, sugar and cooking oil, and cold apartments winter after winter.

The end began in the city of Timișoara. On December 16, 1989, townspeople gathered to stop the eviction of a pastor, László Tőkés; troops fired on them, and within a week the uprising reached Bucharest. It showed how fast public obedience can vanish once people see their neighbors dare to defy a dictator. On December 21 Ceaușescu ordered a mass rally beneath the balcony of the party's Central Committee building, carried live on national television. In mid-speech, for the first time in his rule, the crowd turned on him: boos and jeers rose, his face froze in shock, and every home in Romania watched it happen on state TV. He fled by helicopter and was caught, and on December 25, 1989, Christmas Day, a military tribunal at Târgoviște tried him and Elena in about an hour and had them shot by firing squad.

Like East Germany's Stasi, the Soviet KGB and Albania's Sigurimi, Romania's Securitate was a secret-police force with a wide network of neighborhood informants, enormous for the size of the country, built to defend the state against its own people.

comparative-advantage-in-reverse-what-pr.context_blurb:
In 1817 the English economist David Ricardo showed that voluntary trade can make both sides richer even when one of them is better at producing everything. Two centuries later, the American tariff schedule offers a sharp lesson in what overriding that insight costs, and in who pays the bill.

American tariffs on shoes are not flat. Cheap plastic and canvas sneakers carry duties of 15 to 20 percent, while fine leather dress shoes carry only 5 to 8 percent, and shoppers pay the difference at the checkout. Because poorer families spend a bigger part of their income on such low-end goods, low-income households pay more of this tax. Compare a family earning $200,000 a year with one earning $30,000. Both need shoes, shirts and pants, so the extra dollars the tariff adds are much alike, but for the poor family those dollars are a far larger slice of the budget, and so the poor family loses the bigger share of its income.

In 2002 the trade researcher Edward Gresser of the Progressive Policy Institute documented the pattern in a paper titled Toughest on the Poor. Measured against income, the tariff bill of the bottom fifth of households came to three or four times the burden of the richest fifth. Thomas Sowell of Stanford's Hoover Institution drew the political moral in Basic Economics: the people who claim to defend American workers with tariffs are the ones taxing those workers hardest.

Ricardo's idea is easy to see in miniature. Anna is quicker than Ben at both baking and sign-painting, yet it can still pay for Ben to paint while Anna bakes, and then for the two to trade. Economists call this comparative advantage: each side gains by doing what costs it least to give up, even when the other side is better at everything, and every tariff that overrides it leaves both trading nations poorer than they could have been.

A tariff on imported shirts does not fall on wages or profits directly. It raises the shelf price, so the shopper at the register pays it, which makes a tariff behave much like a consumption tax, a targeted sales tax, and a regressive one at that. The lopsided pattern was no accident. It accumulated, bill by bill, over many decades, because the domestic producers of low-end goods such as footwear and cheap apparel lobbied hardest for protection, while the scattered shoppers who paid never organized.

covid-era-ppe-price-gouging-and-the-mung.context_blurb:
When COVID-19 struck the United States in March 2020, face masks, sanitizer and even toilet rolls vanished from the shelves, and prices began to climb. Most states answered by making it illegal to sell such goods above their old prices. The Duke University economist Michael Munger has spent years explaining why rules like that prolong shortages instead of ending them, and his favorite story involves a truckload of generators.

Laws that forbid selling emergency goods far above their usual price are called anti-price-gouging laws; most states already had them on the books and switched them on as emergencies were declared, with officials threatening fines and jail. Think of a hurricane that strips Florida's stores of bottled water, so the last bottles cost $10 instead of $2. Buyers call it gouging, but economists such as Thomas Sowell point out that the high price is doing a job: it signals sellers everywhere to rush more water to Florida, and fast.

The story comes from 2005. When Hurricane Katrina knocked out power across Mississippi in 2005, John Shepperson of Kentucky bought 19 generators, hired a truck and set off some 600 miles south, meaning to sell them at roughly twice their cost, a markup that would repay his expenses, his labor and his risk. Mississippi police arrested him under the state's anti-gouging law and confiscated the generators, which sat in custody instead of reaching anyone without power.

Bastiat's method sorts the case neatly. What everyone sees is the pleasant, low price on any generator that does get sold. The unseen part is every entrepreneur who never drives supplies into a disaster area, because the reward for doing so has been made a crime. In 2020 a few states briefly declined to enforce their gouging laws on masks and gloves, and their shelves refilled faster; economists such as Steven Horwitz argued that the higher prices told sellers to rush supply in and told buyers not to hoard. Munger packs the lesson into a slogan: in an emergency, he says, gouging is not the problem at all but the solution.

Thomas Sowell, the economist born in 1930 whose Basic Economics is read around the world, names the error at the heart of every such law: it mistakes a price signal for a moral offense, treating information about scarcity as proof of bad character. Munger adds that the real cost falls on a hidden group, the future entrepreneurs who learn from one visible arrest that carrying goods into a stricken area will not be rewarded and may even land them in jail.

So when a storm knocks out a coast's power for a week and generator prices soar, the economist in Bastiat's tradition sees the high price quietly doing its work. It tells suppliers far away that trucks and generators are worth rushing in, and it tells buyers nearby to conserve.

davis-bacon-and-prevailing-wages-paid-to.context_blurb:
In 1931, early in the Great Depression, Congress approved the Davis-Bacon Act, named for its sponsors, Representative Robert Bacon of New York and Senator James Davis of Pennsylvania. It requires that construction workers on federally funded projects be paid the local prevailing wage. Its effects, and the motives behind it, make it a classic case for public-choice economists.

The Department of Labor sets that wage by surveying local pay, and in most cities the survey settles on the union scale as its answer. Paying union rates on every federal highway, school and courthouse makes those projects more expensive, often well above what private builders in the same town pay. Studies by the Congressional Budget Office and the Beacon Hill Institute put the extra cost on federal construction at roughly 10 to 15 percent, which adds up to tens of billions of dollars in any big infrastructure package.

The 1931 debate made the original motive hard to miss. Several of the bill's backers said openly that they wanted to keep Southern Black workers, who were moving north and competing for federal construction jobs at lower wages, off federal building sites. On the House floor Congressman Miles Allgood of Alabama complained of a builder from back home who had won a federal job in New York and brought cheap colored labor north with him, labor that was, in his words, in competition with white labor throughout the country. The racial language later disappeared from talk about the law, but its exclusionary effect on lower-wage newcomers remains built into the mechanism.

Bastiat's lens shows the two sides. The seen is the union jobs on the site; the unseen is the markup every federal taxpayer pays. It fits Mancur Olson's classic pattern exactly: a concentrated benefit for the construction unions, organized and loud, and a dispersed cost for taxpayers, each paying too little to notice. That is why critics in the free-market and public-choice camps, among them Chris Edwards of the Cato Institute, have called for repeal for decades: the law raises the cost of every road, bridge and school the federal government pays for.

denationalisation-of-money-1976-hayeks-c.context_blurb:
In 1976 Friedrich Hayek, the Austrian-born economist who had shared the 1974 Nobel prize, published the most radical monetary proposal of his career. With inflation raging across the Western world, he traced the trouble to a single source, the government's monopoly on money. His remedy was to end the monopoly.

Hayek proposed letting private banks and firms put out money of their own, with customers picking whichever kept its value best, so that every issuer was forced to behave. The idea is called currency competition. The pamphlet came out in London from the Institute of Economic Affairs, Britain's oldest classical-liberal think tank, which Antony Fisher, a businessman who had made his money raising chickens, set up in 1955 on Hayek's own advice after reading The Road to Serfdom.

His single bold proposal was that governments surrender their sole right to issue money and allow private issuers to compete for people's trust. Money, he argued, is a good like any other, and competition checked by consumer choice would supply it better than a state monopoly. The pamphlet's formal title named both the reform and the historical practice behind it: Denationalisation of Money: An Analysis of the Theory and Practice of Concurrent Currencies. Concurrent currencies meant episodes such as nineteenth-century Scotland, where notes from several private banks circulated side by side.

His case rested on the historical record of government monopoly money, from Diocletian's denarius to the Weimar mark of 1923: given enough time, every such currency had been debased or destroyed, because a monopoly issuer under short-run political pressure is always tempted to inflate. What would keep private issuers honest? The same discipline every producer faces: consumers refusing to hold or accept a currency whose value was falling. An issuer whose money lost purchasing power would see it refused and would fail, while one that kept it stable would win business. Hayek predicted that only currencies that held their value would survive, so inflation would fall, and in his enlarged second edition of 1978 he added that a free market in money would settle on a few stable standards rather than an unmanageable crowd of them.

Even Murray Rothbard, who agreed that the state should not run money, drew a line here. He accepted free banking but insisted that any honest free-market money be backed by a commodity such as gold, its notes redeemable for the metal; Hayek's unbacked competing paper went further than Rothbard would. Asked why companies should compete to supply money, a Hayekian answers that the reason is the same one that lets many bakeries sell bread and many firms sell phones. Rivalry hands customers a choice and drives suppliers to serve them well, and the burden falls on the monopoly's defenders to explain why money should be the exception.

Three decades later Bitcoin's defenders, such as Saifedean Ammous in The Bitcoin Standard, hailed the pamphlet as their project's grandfather. But Bitcoin relies on a device unavailable to anyone in 1976: a supply schedule locked by cryptography, which no issuer can inflate, with its cap of 21 million coins and its halvings written into the protocol itself rather than enforced through consumer choice.

dot-com-bust-and-the-housing-bubble-setu.context_blurb:
Between 1995 and 2000 Americans rushed to buy shares in young internet firms, and the Nasdaq index of technology stocks rose about fivefold. Its crash, and the Federal Reserve's response to it, set the stage for the housing bubble and the crisis of 2008. Austrian economists read the whole sequence as one cycle feeding the next.

Any firm with a .com in its name watched its shares soar, though many of those companies had never earned a dollar of profit, and when prices collapsed in March 2000 trillions of dollars of paper wealth disappeared. A run-up of that kind followed by a crash is called a bubble. Back on December 5, 1996, the Fed chairman Alan Greenspan had told an audience at the American Enterprise Institute that investors might be in the grip of irrational exuberance. Yet he left interest rates alone and did nothing to cool the market.

From its peak of 5,048 in March 2000 the Nasdaq fell to 1,114 by October 2002, a loss of 78 percent, roughly three-quarters of its value, and hundreds of dot-com companies failed. The Fed answered with its most aggressive rate cutting in decades. Over two and a half years, from early 2001 to mid-2003, it cut thirteen times, taking its key rate from 6.5 percent down to 1.0 percent, the lowest in 46 years, and it held the rate there until June 2004.

That cheap money had a massive unintended effect: it inflated US housing. Subprime mortgages with low teaser rates drove a boom, and the Case-Shiller index of home prices in twenty cities more than doubled between 2000 and 2006. From 2005 to 2007 the investor Peter Schiff warned on CNBC and other channels that the Fed's low rates were blowing up a housing bubble, while fellow panelists chuckled. Then the housing market collapsed in 2007 and 2008, and he was proven right.

Austrian business cycle theory traces a single chain. Easy money in the 1990s fed the dot-com bubble, and the rate cuts of 2001 to 2003, the answer to that crash, were the direct origin of the 2008 crisis; the Fed, in this reading, solved one bubble by inflating a bigger one. After the crash two Boston Fed economists, Paul Willen and Kristopher Gerardi, dug into the subprime loan data and concluded that the boom grew mainly from a belief, shared by lenders and borrowers alike, that home prices could only go up.

The deeper lesson concerns how a central bank reacts. Each response to a bust plants the seeds of the next one, so there is no escape from the cycle without accepting the liquidation of bad investments that the theory says must come. Greenspan's 1996 speech carries its own moral. A central-bank chair who publicly warns of a bubble but does nothing to restrain it has in effect endorsed the speculation, and markets read his inaction as a green light.

el-salvador-the-first-country-to-make-bi.context_blurb:
On September 7, 2021, El Salvador, a small Central American country, became the first country anywhere to give Bitcoin the status of legal tender, beside the US dollar it already used. The law was the project of its young president, Nayib Bukele, elected in 2019. The experiment set a sovereign state against the international financial institutions built around government money.

Unlike the cash in your pocket, Bitcoin is issued by no government or bank; it is created by computers around the world running the same open software. The Bitcoin Law passed the Legislative Assembly on June 9, 2021, and took effect that September. El Salvador had already given up its own money, the colón, in 2001, adopting the US dollar as its official currency, and Bitcoin was added beside the dollar, not in place of it.

One big hope concerned the Salvadorans working abroad, mostly in the United States, who send billions of dollars home every year through wire services with steep fees: Bitcoin was meant to let them get money to their families faster and more cheaply than banks allowed. Bukele announced the plan in June 2021 in a video message to Bitcoin 2021, a huge conference of Bitcoin enthusiasts and developers in Miami, and pushed the law through within days.

The government launched a free national phone wallet called Chivo, Salvadoran slang for cool, built on Bitcoin's Lightning Network, a quicker payment layer riding above the main chain, so that corner shops could accept tiny payments cheaply. As an incentive, the government gave each adult who signed up $30 in bitcoin, and the bonus drove millions of downloads in the first weeks, though the app had serious early bugs.

The International Monetary Fund urged the country to abandon the law. Its stated reason was not crime or speed but price: Bitcoin's price, the Fund argued, swings far too much to safely back a nation's economy, with risks to fiscal reporting and bank supervision. Bukele mocked the Fund and pressed on. In November 2022 he announced that the country would buy one bitcoin per day for its national reserves, whatever the price, building a treasury steadily instead of trying to time the market.

Bitcoin's supply is capped at 21 million coins by its code, beyond the control of any state or central bank, so El Salvador's move defied the consensus of international financial institutions such as the IMF, which prefer that countries use state-issued money they can influence. In the Austrian reading, any successful national adoption of a money no state controls weakens those institutions' influence. El Salvador also sits on active volcanoes, and Bukele planned to mine Bitcoin with their heat, letting geothermal steam drive generators whose electricity runs the mining computers, starting at the Tecapa volcano. In November 2021 he announced a Bitcoin City near the Conchagua volcano, to be powered the same way and funded by Bitcoin bonds, though building has been slow.

esg-as-regulatory-capture-blackrock-vang.context_blurb: Three enormous US asset managers together manage more than twenty-two trillion dollars in client assets through index funds and other vehicles. Because index funds necessarily hold shares in every company in the index, these three firms collectively hold roughly a fifth to a quarter of the shares of the average S&P 500 company, and they cast proxy votes on behalf of tens of millions of dispersed shareholders. In 2019 two Boston University law professors documented the aggregate voting power of this trio in a widely-cited paper that gave the phenomenon a memorable nickname. Beginning in 2018 the CEO of the largest of the three asset managers began sending an annual public letter to corporate leaders calling on companies to take action on climate, workforce composition, and other items on an investment-labeling framework whose three-letter acronym became ubiquitous in financial media through the early 2020s. Public-choice economists noticed something: this looked structurally like what George Stigler had described in 1971 under the heading of regulatory capture, except that it did not require any formal government regulator. The capture ran through private fiduciary infrastructure. In August 2022 the governor of a large US state led the first prominent state-level pushback by ordering a divestment of state pension funds from one of the firms, and in 2022 the largest manager began offering institutional clients the ability to direct their own share votes. The episode extends Stigler's framework to intermediaries who decide on behalf of dispersed principals.

fdrs-agricultural-adjustment-act-1933-an.context_blurb: In May 1933, in the depths of the Great Depression, President Franklin Roosevelt signed a landmark New Deal law designed to raise farm prices by reducing crop acreage and livestock populations. Under its emergency hog program in the fall of that year the federal government paid farmers to slaughter roughly six million pigs, many of them piglets, with much of the meat rendered into fertilizer at a moment when millions of Americans in the same cities were in breadlines. The Agriculture Secretary who had to defend the slaughter on national radio was booed, and would later become Roosevelt's third-term vice president. The policy is the archetypal Bastiat case: the visible benefit was higher prices for farmers whose remaining stock went to market; the invisible destruction was the food that never reached the hungry. In January 1936 the Supreme Court struck down the original statute as an unconstitutional use of the taxing power. A 1938 successor law was written to survive the court challenge and still forms the backbone of today's omnibus farm legislation Congress reauthorizes roughly every five years. Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz argued in A Monetary History of the United States that the New Deal's supply-restriction programs, by raising costs during a period of monetary contraction, prolonged the depression rather than ending it. Amity Shlaes reintroduced the Rothbard-Friedman critique to a general audience in a 2007 book. The pig slaughter is the vivid centerpiece of a wider political-economy pattern Mancur Olson later made explicit.

fiscal-stimulus-and-the-multiplier-the-p.context_blurb: In January 2009 the incoming Obama administration's Council of Economic Advisers published a memo predicting that if Congress passed the then-pending $787 billion American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, US unemployment would peak below a specific level. The memo was signed by the incoming CEA chair and the vice president's chief economist, and its forecast rested on a numerical assumption about how much extra GDP each stimulus dollar would produce. By October 2009 unemployment was well above the memo's peak forecast. The reason, according to economists who redid the arithmetic with more realistic frictions, was that the multiplier assumption had been generous: Cogan, Cwik, Taylor, and Wieland recalculated it with standard New-Keynesian crowding-out and got numbers well below 1. Robert Barro, using World War II as the biggest natural-experiment shock, estimated the peacetime defense-spending multiplier in a similar range. Valerie Ramey's vector-autoregression work found peacetime civilian multipliers below one as well. The Bastiat-style objection at the core of all this is that any stimulus dollar had to come from somewhere specific: it was taxed from a household, borrowed from a lender, or printed by the central bank. Henry Hazlitt's 1946 Economics in One Lesson devotes a chapter to the Bastiat objection whose four-word title compresses the whole point. An earlier version of the same objection appeared in a 1932 letter from four British economists including Hayek to a London newspaper. The deep move is naming the invisible foregone private spending: the modern name for Bastiat's UNSEEN is crowding-out.

friedman-in-chile-1975-and-the-chicago-b.context_blurb: In March 1975 Milton Friedman made a six-day trip to Chile at the invitation of a private Chilean foundation. He met the country's military ruler for about forty-five minutes, delivered public lectures, and returned to Chicago. The visit became controversial because Chile at that moment was ruled by a general who had come to power in a September 1973 coup against the elected socialist government. Friedman replied to his critics in a 1976 Newsweek letter describing the regime using a specific sharp phrase and comparing his visit to a doctor treating a patient in a country whose government he disapproved of. The deeper story was already underway. Starting in 1955 the University of Chicago had run an exchange program with Chile's Catholic University that had, by the mid-1970s, trained roughly twenty-five Chilean economists in Chicago-style price theory. These economists took over economic policy in the second half of the 1970s and ran a market-reform program: tariff cuts, privatizations, opening to foreign investment, a privatized pension system. Chilean poverty fell from roughly forty-five percent in 1973 to around ten percent by 2010 by national statistics agency and World Bank measures. In 1988 a national plebiscite voted the general out and the country returned to democracy; successor center-left governments retained the market-economy framework for the next thirty years. Friedman visited Communist China in 1980 and had earlier given similar advice in the USSR and Yugoslavia without generating comparable protest. The full arc of the 1973-2010s Chilean story is a real natural experiment in economic-reform outcomes.

ftx-the-second-lesson-at-massive-scale.context_blurb: In November 2022 the world's second-largest cryptocurrency exchange, headquartered in the Bahamas and valued at thirty-two billion dollars at its peak, stopped honoring customer withdrawals and filed for bankruptcy days later. Its founder was a former Jane Street quant trader in his late twenties, MIT-educated, widely known by his initials, who had also founded a sister trading firm run at various times by Caroline Ellison. A specific crypto trade publication published a leaked balance sheet on November 2 showing that the sister firm's largest single asset was not a normal reserve of outside tokens but a stockpile of the exchange's own in-house token. The world's largest exchange by trading volume announced days later that it would sell its holdings of that in-house token, triggering a classic bank run that hit the exchange within hours. The operational fact that made the collapse a fraud rather than merely a bankruptcy was documented after the fact: customer funds had been commingled with the sister firm's trading positions and used to cover its losses. The founder was convicted on seven counts of fraud and conspiracy in November 2023 and sentenced to twenty-five years in federal prison in March 2024. He had publicly identified his personal ethics with a specific movement whose stated aim was to do the most good possible with one's resources. The collapse echoed a Bitcoin-community slogan about self-custody: every customer who had trusted the exchange lost access, and every customer who had kept hold of the keys was untouched. The failure mode is the same one that destroyed Mt Gox in 2014.

greenspans-1-and-the-2005-no-bubble-spee.context_blurb: Alan Greenspan served as chair of the Federal Reserve from August 1987 through January 2006, longer than anyone in modern history, spanning four US presidents. After the dot-com crash of 2000 and 2001, the Fed under Greenspan took the federal funds rate from six and a half percent down to a historic low and held it there for a year, from mid-2003 to mid-2004. The extended low policy rate poured cash into the American housing market, where prices had risen at roughly the rate of general inflation for decades and began rising at double-digit rates in coastal metros. Two large subprime originators wrote enormous volumes of exotic mortgages during the boom. On October 27, 2005, at a specific industry conference, Greenspan publicly dismissed concerns about a national housing bubble, acknowledging some local froth but arguing the market was heterogeneous and so a coordinated national bubble was unlikely. Austrian analysts, drawing on the business-cycle theory Ludwig von Mises had first developed in 1912 and Hayek had extended in 1931, had been warning since 2003 that artificially low rates were producing exactly the kind of malinvestment the theory predicts. In October 2008 congressional testimony, after the crisis had struck, the retired chair made an extraordinary admission about a flaw in his belief that self-interested bankers would protect their own institutions from ruin. Few people recall that Greenspan himself, in a 1966 essay in Ayn Rand's Objectivist newsletter, had argued explicitly for a gold-based monetary system against the inflationary logic of fiat money. His career illustrates the Austrian point about cheap credit and the correction that always follows.

hans-hermann-hoppe-democracy-the-god-tha.context_blurb: Hans-Hermann Hoppe is a German-born economist who took his 1974 Frankfurt doctorate under one of the leading left-wing philosophers of the twentieth century, then moved steadily rightward and emigrated to the United States in 1986 to work alongside Murray Rothbard at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas. He taught there until his retirement in 2008. His best-known book was published in 2001 by Transaction Publishers and advances an argument that has made him controversial even within the Austrian tradition: that hereditary rule, judged purely by the incentive structure it imposes on the ruler, produces better long-run governance behavior than a competitive electoral system does. The argument turns on time-preference, the question of how heavily an officeholder weighs the present against the future given the length of his tenure. Hoppe frames the difference between a monarch and a democratic politician through a property-rights analogy about who owns and who rents the state itself. A separate 1988 argument of his, called argumentation ethics, claims that the very act of arguing already presupposes self-ownership. He founded the Property and Freedom Society in 2006 as an annual libertarian conference that meets each summer in a Turkish coastal resort town. His 1989 book had already laid out his systematic praxeological-ethics defense of private property against socialism. Within the Austrian tradition itself, scholars like Peter Boettke at George Mason and Joseph Salerno at Pace have accepted parts of Hoppe's incentive analysis without endorsing his political conclusion.

import-quotas-the-1980s-japanese-auto-ve.context_blurb: In May 1981 the Reagan administration negotiated an agreement with Japan capping Japanese passenger-car exports to the United States at roughly one point seven million vehicles per year, below the roughly one point nine million actually sold in 1980. The restriction was labeled voluntary because Japan self-imposed the cap under diplomatic pressure, which let both sides avoid a formal US tariff. The point was to protect the three big Detroit manufacturers, who had been losing market share to Japanese imports. Robert Crandall of the Brookings Institution later studied the policy and estimated a four-figure consumer cost per car in the United States across the decade; subsequent work put the total annual consumer cost well into the billions. The policy produced one unintended consequence economists find especially instructive. Because the cap was set in vehicles rather than in dollars, each Japanese car exported to the US had to earn more profit per unit. Honda, Toyota, and Nissan responded by moving systematically up-market: models like the Accord, the Camry, and the Maxima grew larger, better-equipped, and more expensive through the 1980s. The money that would have been a US tariff revenue flowed instead to the Japanese automakers as extra profit on each car, in the form of what economists call quota rent.

james-m-buchanan-tennessee-farm-boy-to-n.context_blurb: James McGill Buchanan was born in October 1919 on a small farm outside Murfreesboro, Tennessee, the grandson of a Reconstruction-era governor. He paid his way through a state teachers college, served under Admiral Nimitz on wartime Navy staff in Honolulu, and entered graduate school at the University of Chicago in 1945 on the GI Bill. Buchanan arrived at Chicago as a Southern rural Democrat sympathetic to New Deal redistribution and left, as he put it, a market-order man. He later credited six weeks in a specific price-theory course under a specific Chicago mentor for the whole conversion. In 1957 he co-founded a research center at the University of Virginia with G. Warren Nutter; in 1969 he and Gordon Tullock founded a new center at Virginia Tech; in 1983 the center moved to George Mason University in Fairfax, where Buchanan spent the rest of his career. He spent a 1955-56 Fulbright year in Rome, working with Luigi Einaudi and the Italian public-finance tradition, which shaped his sense that fiscal rules sit above day-to-day politics. In October 1986 the Royal Swedish Academy named Buchanan the year's economics laureate for his development of the contractual and constitutional bases of economic and political decision-making. He insisted on displaying a portrait of his Chicago mentor at the Stockholm ceremonies.

joseph-salerno-and-the-calculation-debat.context_blurb: Joseph Salerno is a Brooklyn-born Pace University economist who has become the most persistent modern scholar of the 1920 Mises calculation debate. He has edited the flagship modern Austrian scholarly journal since its founding in 1998, a journal distinct from the older Review of Austrian Economics edited by Peter Boettke. The dispute Salerno has championed is a live intra-Austrian question about how to read Mises's founding essay. There are two broadly-accepted interpretations. One, closer to a reading developed in the mid-1940s by Friedrich Hayek and extended by Israel Kirzner and Don Lavoie, frames Mises's argument primarily as a knowledge problem, with calculation impossible because the dispersed information needed to run an economy cannot be gathered in time. The other, which Salerno has defended with care in a 1990 article in the Review of Austrian Economics that shifted majority Austrian opinion within the Mises Institute tradition, reads Mises more strictly: the core claim is specifically that without real market prices for producer goods, no monetary cost comparison is possible, so the calculation problem is a monetary problem, not primarily a knowledge problem. In 2010 Salerno collected his applied-Misesian monetary essays into a book from the Mises Institute. In 2004 he edited a scholar's edition reuniting Rothbard's 1962 treatise with its originally excised political-economy volume. Salerno's work shows how a working Austrian scholar reads a founding text closely enough to recover arguments and distinctions that even friendly interpreters sometimes fold together.

karl-marx-and-the-close-of-his-system--1.context_blurb: Karl Marx died in London in 1883 without finishing his masterwork Das Kapital. Only Volume 1, published in 1867, was in print; Volumes 2 and 3 existed as boxes of handwritten manuscripts his collaborator published posthumously, Volume 2 in 1885 and Volume 3 in 1894. Volume 1 had laid down a sharp claim that the ratio in which two goods trade is set by the socially necessary labor hours embodied in each. Attentive readers had noticed immediately that this claim did not match observed market prices, because capital-heavy industries do not sell their output at labor-time ratios. The gap between the two claims had a name among nineteenth-century commentators: the transformation problem. Volume 3, when it finally appeared, was expected to transform the labor-values of Volume 1 into the actual prices of production in the real economy. Two years later the Austrian economist Eugen Boehm-Bawerk published a scorching reply in a festschrift honoring an older German-tradition economist. His charge was precise: not that Marx had failed an empirical test but that Marx's own two volumes contradicted each other on their own terms. In 1904 a young Marxist named Rudolf Hilferding, who would later serve as Weimar Germany's finance minister, published the standard Marxist reply. In 1949 the American Marxist economist Paul Sweezy compiled both essays into a single English volume that remains the standard source. Later groups of Marxist economists, Duncan Foley and Fred Moseley among them, have offered what they call the New Interpretation, which concedes the 1896 charge and rebuilds from different Marx passages. The whole eighty-year arc is a case study in how one careful essay can close an academic argument.

kirznerian-entrepreneurship-applied-jobs.context_blurb: Israel Kirzner is an American Austrian economist whose 1973 University of Chicago Press book defined the entrepreneur as the person alert to profit opportunities others have missed. His definition sits between two older ones: Frank Knight's figure who principally bears risk, and Joseph Schumpeter's figure whose innovations creatively destroy old industries. Kirzner's category is different. The Kirznerian entrepreneur sees an opportunity sitting there in plain sight, which other competitors could have seen with the same information and the same technology, and acts on it. Kirzner was a direct student of Ludwig von Mises at New York University, where Mises taught from 1945 to his death in 1973. The Kirznerian lens can be applied to three of the most spectacular American companies of the last three decades. Each founder has a story that fits the framework: an integration opportunity in consumer electronics, a cost assumption about disposability in the launch industry that had gone unchallenged for forty years, and a starting product category whose logistical features were perfect for internet-scale retail. Kirzner received the Global Award for Entrepreneurship Research in 2006, the field's major international honor, though he never received a Nobel. Real entrepreneurs blend elements of all three Austrian theories: alertness, risk-bearing, and innovation. The point of a framework like Kirzner's is not to label a founder; it is to clarify which theory fits which specific move inside the founder's story.

lightning-network-micropayments-on-top-o.context_blurb: Bitcoin's main chain was deliberately designed to settle slowly and securely rather than quickly and cheaply. It adds one block every ten minutes and each block holds only a few thousand transactions, which works for large transfers and settlement but makes it ill-suited to buying a two-dollar coffee. The problem had an elegant solution in the form of a second layer built on top of the base chain, proposed in a January 2016 white paper by two Bitcoin developers. Two parties who want to transact repeatedly open a payment channel by committing some Bitcoin to a two-party smart contract on the base chain; they can then send payments back and forth off-chain, as many as they want at essentially no cost, and only close the channel back onto the base chain at the end to record the final balance. The design also solved the harder problem of letting people pay each other without opening a direct channel to each counterparty: payments can route through a graph of intermediaries, each of whom charges a small voluntary fee set by competition among node operators rather than by any central body. The network was the engine behind one Central American country's state-launched Bitcoin wallet in 2021, which let small merchants accept Bitcoin for ordinary purchases, and an American developer who had built one of the first Lightning payment apps appeared alongside the country's president at the June 2021 conference where the legal-tender law was announced.

mancur-olson-the-logic-of-collective-act.context_blurb: In 1965 Harvard University Press published a short book that began as a North Dakota farm boy's PhD dissertation and permanently changed the way economists and political scientists talk about group behavior. The book explained a puzzle that had bothered careful observers for decades: why do policies with large diffuse costs and small concentrated benefits so reliably survive, even in democracies where the voter majority would be better off if the policy were repealed? The author's answer identified a specific game-theoretic problem in large groups, where each individual has an incentive to let others bear the cost of producing a shared benefit. Readers often misread the book as claiming that large groups never organize. The actual argument identified one mechanism that lets some large groups succeed anyway: private benefits available only to members. A classic textbook example is a large voluntary organization whose members join partly to get discounted insurance, hotel rates, and travel discounts. The author went on to write two more big books. A 1982 Yale volume applied the framework to explain the economic growth differences across the postwar developed economies; a 2000 posthumous book extended it to explain the gap between rich and poor nations. The deep move is a Bastiat move about which side of a policy organizes and which side never does.

microstrategy-the-first-corporate-treasu.context_blurb: In August 2020, in the middle of the COVID-era Federal Reserve balance-sheet expansion, a Virginia-headquartered business-intelligence software company announced that it was converting a chunk of its corporate cash reserve into Bitcoin. It was the first US public company to do so at scale, and the founder and long-time CEO who steered the move became the most public corporate Bitcoin advocate of the next five years. The initial purchase in August 2020 was followed by many more, financed by convertible-bond offerings during the 2022 bear market when the firm's accumulated Bitcoin position was underwater on paper by billions. By early 2026 the company had accumulated more than two hundred thousand Bitcoin, the largest corporate Bitcoin holding in the world. In August 2025 it completed a legal name change and adopted a new logo featuring the orange Bitcoin color, cementing the shift from its old identity as a software firm to its new identity as a treasury vehicle. The public case for the strategy is Austrian in every important respect. The CEO points to a monetary distortion first described by the eighteenth-century thinker Richard Cantillon, in which new money reaches different holders at different speeds and benefits whoever gets it first. His move inverts a standard corporate-finance default: he argues that if directors have a fiduciary duty to preserve shareholder value, and dollar cash certainly loses purchasing power at a debasing central bank, then holding a scarce non-state asset is the fiduciary-consistent trade. The strategy has had imitators that have risen and sometimes fallen in its wake.

mises-s-critique-of-interventionism.context_blurb: By the late 1920s the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises had spent a decade arguing that the mixed economy of subsidies, price controls, and targeted taxes was not a stable third option between capitalism and socialism but an unstable disequilibrium that must retreat toward markets or advance to further intervention. In 1929 he collected the argument in a German-language book whose title and subtitle set out the project. On April 18, 1950 Mises stood before the University Club in New York and gave the compact restatement of his three-decade case, printed days later in a financial weekly. The lecture walked the audience through a stylized milk example to show why partial intervention cannot rest: a government that caps the retail price of a food item will see the supply contract, and in response must cap the price of the feed used to produce the food item, then the price of the fuel used to transport the feed, then the wages paid in the input industries, until the state has effectively taken over every price in the economy. Mises argued that control is indivisible: either consumers direct production through the prices they are willing to pay or the state does through decree, and the middle position cannot hold. He closed with a famous short sentence that has been quoted ever since as the compact statement of the whole position. In 1987 the American economist Robert Higgs published an Oxford study of American federal growth across the twentieth century documenting a specific one-way asymmetry: governments that grew in a crisis never fully returned to their pre-crisis size afterward.

murray-rothbard-who-he-was.context_blurb: Murray Rothbard was born on March 2, 1926 and died on January 7, 1995. He entered Columbia at sixteen, earned a BA at nineteen, took his Columbia PhD in 1956 with a dissertation on the Panic of 1819, and by the late 1950s had become the second generation of the American Austrian school. His father David was a chemist who had emigrated from Poland; the family were Jewish immigrants to the Bronx. From the mid-1950s Rothbard attended Ludwig von Mises's private seminar at New York University, paid for by a classical-liberal donor fund. Mainstream American economics departments refused to hire him for the first thirty years of his career; he taught part-time at a Brooklyn engineering school from 1966 to 1986 while writing the Austrian tradition's flagship American treatise. In 1986 he finally moved to a full economics chair at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas, where he stayed until his death. He helped co-found two of the most influential libertarian institutions of the century, the Washington think tank in 1977 and the Austrian-focused academic institute in Auburn, Alabama in 1982, each as a different wing of the same movement. He coined a specific term for his own political system, a stateless private-property order defended by voluntary institutions, which distinguished his position from the minarchism of Nozick and the minimal-state objectivism of Rand. His 1973 Macmillan popular manifesto introduced his system to general readers; his four-volume history of American colonial life and the Revolution, published between 1975 and 1979 with a fifth volume assembled posthumously in 2019, is his largest work of American history.

nimby-political-economy-palo-alto-zoning.context_blurb: In Silicon Valley the paradigm case of local homeowners successfully blocking new housing is a small city that houses Stanford University, where the median home price has approached three million dollars. Roughly ninety-four percent of its residential land is zoned exclusively for single-family detached homes, which makes apartment construction practically illegal across almost the whole city. The three-letter shorthand for the pattern in which existing local homeowners organize to block new housing in their neighborhoods, even when a region's overall housing shortage produces high rents and long commutes, has become standard political-science vocabulary. Harvard urban economist Edward Glaeser and Wharton's Joseph Gyourko coined a term for the wedge between the actual construction cost of housing in supply-constrained cities and its market price, estimating it in the range of thirty to sixty percent in Bay Area cities. In Mancur Olson's framework, applied to this case, existing homeowners are the concentrated beneficiary group that organizes; the dispersed victims are families priced out to distant commuter cities or out of California entirely, who cannot vote in the city and often never knew that a specific project would have housed them. A counter-coalition began forming around 2015-16 under a different four-letter acronym. California passed a 2021 state law allowing homeowners to build a duplex on single-family lots over local objection, and the city of Minneapolis in 2018 became the first major US city to eliminate single-family-only zoning citywide. One large Sun Belt city produced actual measured rent declines through a 2019-2024 permitting boom. Japan's national zoning system, which permits substantial by-right construction, has kept Tokyo housing prices comparatively stable.

operation-twist-and-qe3-2011-14.context_blurb: On September 21, 2011 the Federal Reserve announced a program to sell four hundred billion dollars of short-dated Treasuries while buying the same quantity of long-dated ones, flattening the yield curve without expanding the balance sheet. The program borrowed its name from a Kennedy-era Treasury-Fed program of 1961 that had first tried the yield-curve-flattening technique, originally for a different policy purpose. One year later, on September 13, 2012, the Fed launched its third round of large-scale asset purchases, initially committing forty billion dollars per month in mortgage-backed-security purchases with no announced cap. A market strategist coined a now-standard nickname for the program that stuck immediately across financial media. In December 2012 the program was expanded to add forty-five billion dollars per month in longer-dated Treasury purchases, bringing total monthly Fed asset buying to a very large monthly figure. The program ran until October 2014, when a new Fed chair, the first woman to lead the Federal Reserve, announced the taper-and-end. By late 2014 the Fed's balance sheet had grown roughly fivefold from its pre-2008 level. Austrian critics warned throughout the era that an expansion of this scale was setting up a future price event once money velocity recovered, pointing to a Cantillon pattern in which asset prices rise first and consumer prices follow with a long lag. The 2021-2023 consumer-price wave, arriving more than a decade after the first round, fit the Austrian prediction. There is also a public-choice point: when central-bank monthly purchases exceed the annual GDP of several small countries, the choice of which assets to buy is inescapably political, not merely technical.

peter-schiff-and-the-gold-versus-bitcoin.context_blurb: Peter Schiff is an American stockbroker who runs the firm Euro Pacific Capital. He has been publicly bullish on gold since the early 2000s and became widely known outside the gold community after making a correct prediction about an American financial crisis on live cable television in the years just before it came true. His father, an Austrian-economics writer who died while serving a federal prison sentence in 2015, had shaped his economic worldview. Schiff wrote a 2007 book laying out the prediction he had been making on television; videos of the 2006-07 cable appearances became a viral YouTube compilation after the crash arrived. Since roughly 2013 Schiff has been Bitcoin's most persistent critic in the sound-money community. His central argument against Bitcoin points to one specific property gold has that Bitcoin does not: a long history of non-monetary use, from jewelry to industrial applications to five thousand years of recognition across cultures. His standard debate opponent since 2020 has been the executive who made the largest corporate-treasury Bitcoin purchases in history, and the two have exchanged positions in dozens of recorded conversations. His opponent's counter-argument concedes that Bitcoin is new but denies that intrinsic non-monetary value is what actually makes something money, pointing to properties like scarcity, divisibility, portability, and verifiability as the real monetary tests. Schiff reliably brings up an Austrian-tradition argument about how money must originate historically, which his opponent concedes is a substantive argument requiring serious reply. The valuable thing about the exchange is that both men state and defend their positions honestly in public.

politics-without-romance-buchanans-nobel.context_blurb: When James Buchanan sat down to describe what the public-choice school actually did, he coined a three-word phrase that has served as its shorthand ever since. The phrase was the title of a 1979 lecture Buchanan delivered at a Vienna research institute, later widely reprinted. The romance to be stripped was a widespread mid-century habit in welfare economics of comparing imperfect real markets against idealized government interventions, as if political actors somehow escaped the ordinary self-interest that economics assumes for consumers and firms. Buchanan's move was simple and devastating: if we assume ordinary self-interest for consumers and firms, we must assume it for politicians and bureaucrats too. The symmetric treatment produced a whole category of policy breakdown that mirrors the market pathologies of the welfare-economics textbooks, which public-choice calls government failure. Specific mechanisms include regulatory capture, rent-seeking, agency budget maximization, and rational voter ignorance. Thomas Sowell, writing across many books, condensed Buchanan's whole comparative move into a two-word question a critic should always ask when someone claims the market has failed and the government should act. Buchanan credited an older Hungarian-born LSE development economist for coining the closely-related phrase the romantic view of the state well before Buchanan wrote his own. The phrase works as a diagnostic test, not a slogan.

price-gouging-laws-the-generator-that-ne.context_blurb: Hurricane Fran cut power to a million people around Raleigh, North Carolina in September 1996. Four men trucked bagged ice from Goldsboro and sold it at seven times its usual price to residents without electricity for food storage; the police arrested them on the spot, and the crowd that had been waiting in line applauded as they were cuffed. Duke University economist Michael Munger wrote the night up for the Library of Economics and Liberty under a two-word title taken from what the crowd did. Most American states punish merchants who raise prices on water, fuel, and generators after a disaster. Florida's statute does not run all the time: it switches on when the governor declares a state of emergency, and defines unlawful prices in terms of a gross disparity with the previous month's average. A classic case is the Kentucky man who watched Hurricane Katrina coverage in 2005, bought nineteen generators, rented a truck, drove about six hundred miles to Mississippi, and was jailed for four days while the generators sat in police custody rather than reaching anyone who needed them. Hayek's 1945 essay on how a price change moves information through a market shows what the anti-gouging statutes actually silence. Munger has argued against the laws for two decades, and on the economics podcast EconTalk he reduced the position to one sentence about the relationship between permitting high prices now and achieving low prices later. The deep Bastiat move is to name the unseen: every generator sitting in a warehouse two states away that stays there because the signal to bring it has been criminalized.

proof-of-work-vs-proof-of-stake-the-ethe.context_blurb: On September 15, 2022 Ethereum, the second-largest cryptocurrency by market capitalization, completed the largest scheduled software upgrade ever performed on a live financial network. It transitioned off the energy-hungry consensus mechanism that Bitcoin invented and that Ethereum had itself used since launch, onto a new mechanism in which the right to add the next block is assigned not by burning electricity but by locking up a quantity of the cryptocurrency itself. Ethereum Foundation figures put the energy reduction at roughly ninety-nine point nine five percent. Ethereum's founder, who had published its white paper in late 2013, had argued for the switch since Ethereum's earliest design discussions. The most common Bitcoin-community critique of the new mechanism is that it recreates a specific pre-Bitcoin monetary property: those who start with the most tokens have the most power to add blocks, entrench their position, and shape network rules, without any external physical check equivalent to the electricity a miner must burn. The critique rests on an economist's attack called the nothing-at-stake problem, in which validators can costlessly sign multiple competing chains at once because no real-world resource is spent per signature. The chair of the US Securities and Exchange Commission in 2023 suggested that many of the new tokens could fall under US investor-protection statutes. Bitcoin remains on the original mechanism as a core design principle: the electricity cost is not a bug but an external real-world commitment that anchors the network to physical reality. Two cryptocurrencies descended from Bitcoin's codebase persisted on the original mechanism past the 2022 upgrade. The empirical verdict will take decades of live operation across attacks and crashes.

rai-stones-of-yap-the-sunken-money-still.context_blurb: For centuries, villagers on a small group of Micronesian islands used massive round limestone discs as their circulating money. Some were over twelve feet across and weighed several tons. The islands had no limestone of their own; the discs had been carved from aragonite on an island about two hundred and fifty miles away and transported home across the open ocean by outrigger canoe. Once installed, a disc was generally too heavy to move for later transactions. When ownership changed hands, the villagers simply agreed in public that the stone now belonged to someone else, while the physical stone stayed exactly where it was. In the famous Yap sunken-stone story, a canoe crew bringing a particularly large disc home ran into a storm and the disc slid off into deep water; the crew returned and testified to its size and quality, and the villagers agreed that the stone was still valuable, still ownable, and still transferable. In 1991 Milton Friedman retold the story in an essay later collected in his book Money Mischief, drawing a direct parallel to how one New York Federal Reserve staff could shift national gold-ownership entries by moving bars between drawers inside the same vault. The deep lesson, which the cypherpunks later drew too, is that money is a ledger, and the physical container of the ledger is only a secondary engineering choice. Nick Szabo pointed out that the costly open-ocean carving of a disc is a physical analog of Bitcoin's cryptographic proof-of-work.

right-to-try-and-the-fda-from-peltzman-t.context_blurb: In 1973 the Chicago-trained economist Sam Peltzman published a Journal of Political Economy paper studying the effects of a 1962 amendment to the US Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act that had imposed new efficacy requirements for FDA approval, passed in response to a specific European sedative tragedy. Peltzman found a visible benefit (prevented tragedies of that specific kind) and an invisible cost: patients dying while safe and effective drugs sat in a longer approval queue. The move is Bastiat's SEEN versus UNSEEN applied to drug regulation. In May 2018 the federal Right-to-Try Act was signed into law, giving terminally-ill patients access to drugs that had passed Phase I safety trials but not yet received full approval; George Mason University economist Alex Tabarrok has been a leading academic advocate for FDA reform in that direction. A more recent voice is a UCSF hematologist-oncologist whose 2020 Johns Hopkins book argued that many drugs approved through accelerated pathways on surrogate endpoints have not actually delivered survival improvement. His move is to require the outcome that matters rather than proxy measures that often do not translate. The FDA sits inside a two-sided error problem: approving an unsafe drug gets front-page coverage, while blocking a lifesaving one is invisible. The 2016 bipartisan Cures Act and the December 2020 emergency pathway for COVID vaccines both expanded accelerated-approval tools.

saifedean-ammous-the-bitcoin-standard-th.context_blurb: Saifedean Ammous is a Lebanese-Palestinian economist with a Columbia PhD from 2011 who, after years as a tenured professor at Lebanese American University in Beirut, has become the most widely-read modern advocate for treating Bitcoin as sound money in the Austrian tradition. His 2018 Wiley book has since become the best-selling Bitcoin book of all time, translated into more than forty languages. Its central move is to build on an older Austrian tradition that classifies goods by how hard they are to produce more of, and to apply a specific ratio from monetary economics that measures how much of a thing already exists against how much new flow is added each year. Applied to Bitcoin, the argument reaches a dramatic conclusion about Bitcoin's monetary properties over time, because new issuance is cut in half by protocol roughly every four years. In 2021 Ammous published a sequel focused on what fiat currencies have done to the world since Nixon closed the gold window in 1971, from monetary inflation to artificial-food industrialization to debased family and cultural formation. In 2020, during COVID lockdowns, Ammous parted company with the tenured position he had held, refusing the mandatory online-teaching regime; he built a subscription platform of his own to deliver his Austrian-economics course directly, which has grown into a serious teaching institution. Ammous's independent teaching work is most often compared, by his students, to the modern American home of Rothbardian Austrian economics in Alabama.

school-choice-milton-friedmans-1955-vouc.context_blurb: In 1955 the Chicago economist Milton Friedman published an essay titled The Role of Government in Education, later reprinted as a chapter of his 1962 book Capitalism and Freedom. The essay argued that government financing of schooling might be justified on externality grounds, but that government production of schooling did not follow from that justification. His proposal was for a transferable instrument parents could redeem at any accredited school of their choice, including private and religious ones, rather than for a specific district-assigned public school. Since 1970, real US K-12 per-pupil spending has approximately tripled, while scores on the National Assessment of Educational Progress long-term-trend assessment have remained essentially flat. The first urban voucher program in the United States launched in a Midwestern city in 1990, championed by a Democratic state legislator who had been a welfare mother and signed into law by a Republican governor. In 2002 the US Supreme Court upheld a Rust Belt city's voucher program on the reasoning that aid flowed through private parental choice rather than directly to religious institutions. Milton and Rose Friedman founded a foundation in 1996, in the last decade of Milton's life, dedicated to the one policy application he considered his most important. A wave of US state Education Savings Account laws in 2023-2024 made K-12 school choice broadly available for the first time in US history across several states.

silk-road-bitcoins-first-widely-known-us.context_blurb: From February 2011 to October 2013 an online marketplace operating on the Tor anonymity network sold many kinds of illicit goods, most infamously drugs, and used Bitcoin as its exclusive currency. It became the first widely known use case for Bitcoin outside hobbyist circles. The founder, a young American libertarian named Ross Ulbricht, ran the site under a pseudonym drawn from William Goldman's novel The Princess Bride, where the identity is meant to pass from one operator to the next so no single individual is ever caught. On October 1, 2013 the FBI arrested Ulbricht in a very specific public location, the science-fiction section of a San Francisco public library branch, so it could seize his laptop while it was still unlocked and logged into the site's administrator interface. He was convicted in February 2015 on seven counts including drug trafficking conspiracy and money laundering, and in May 2015 received a sentence of life in prison without parole. After nearly ten years of advocacy for his release by libertarians and Bitcoin-community activists, a US president commuted his sentence in January 2025. Within the early Bitcoin community the use of Bitcoin on the site split opinion. Some celebrated that the technology worked as designed, offering censorship-resistant payments no intermediary could block. Others worried that the association with illegal activity would damage Bitcoin's broader prospects. The episode raises questions about proportionality of sentence and about censorship-resistance as a protocol-level design property.

sowell-on-discrimination-and-disparities.context_blurb: In 2018 Thomas Sowell published Discrimination and Disparities, aimed at a line of reasoning common in the news: where two groups end up unequal, someone must have treated one of them worse. The book argues that a difference in outcomes tells you something has differed between the two groups, and not yet what that something is. Sowell's favorite kinds of counter-examples are minorities that were legally restricted, barred from professions, and sometimes attacked in riots, and that nonetheless ended up with higher measured incomes than the host populations around them. Lebanese merchant families across West Africa, Indian merchant families across East Africa, and ethnic-Chinese communities across Southeast Asia all fit this pattern. Sowell argues that the pattern reveals the portability of human capital: trading skills, business habits, educational traditions, and commercial networks travel with people and keep working in new countries. Between 1994 and 1998 he published three linked volumes on race, migration, and conquest built on fifteen years of international travel and research. His 2018 book sharpens a specific analytical move about one English word that has been quietly doing two different jobs: there is a sense of the word that means fact-based sorting on real qualifications, and a second sense that means arbitrary aversion to a group.
